```{r stats-helpers, include=FALSE}
# ---- Statistics boxes ------------------------------------------------------
# Every number in the "Statistics" boxes comes from output/paper/, written by
# the last section of code/02-05 (run with code/run_all.R). pn() stops the build if a number
# is missing, so a renamed key cannot silently drop a value.
paper_dir <- file.path("..", "..", "output", "paper")
paper_nums <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(
  list.files(paper_dir, pattern = "_numbers\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE),
  readr::read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE,
  col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character())
)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(estimate, ci_low, ci_high, statistic, df1, df2, p_value, n), as.numeric))
pn <- function(key) {
  d <- paper_nums[paper_nums$key == key, ]
  if (nrow(d) != 1) stop("pn(): no single number called ", key)
  d
}
fp   <- function(p) if (is.na(p)) "NA" else if (p < 0.001) "*p* < 0.001" else sprintf("*p* = %.3f", p)
fF   <- function(k, digits = 1) { d <- pn(k); sprintf("F~%s,%s~ = %.*f, %s", round(d$df1), round(d$df2), digits, d$statistic, fp(d$p_value)) }
fchi <- function(k) { d <- pn(k); sprintf("χ²~%s~ = %.1f, %s", round(d$df1), d$statistic, fp(d$p_value)) }
fci  <- function(k, digits = 2) { d <- pn(k); sprintf("%.*f; 95%% CI %.*f–%.*f; %s", digits, d$estimate, digits, d$ci_low, digits, d$ci_high, fp(d$p_value)) }
est  <- function(k, digits = 2) sprintf("%.*f", digits, pn(k)$estimate)
frac <- function(k) { d <- pn(k); sprintf("%d of %d", as.integer(d$statistic), as.integer(d$n)) }
cnt  <- function(k, which = c("estimate", "statistic")) { d <- pn(k); sprintf("%d", as.integer(d[[match.arg(which)]])) }
nn   <- function(k) sprintf("%d", as.integer(pn(k)$n))
sens_tbl <- readr::read_csv(table_file("22b_sensitivity_wound_growth.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
sens_p <- function(resp, version) { d <- sens_tbl[sens_tbl$response == resp & sens_tbl$version == version, ]; stopifnot(nrow(d) == 1); fp(d$p_value) }
tank_txt <- function(lab) {
  d <- pn(paste0("budding_per_tank_", lab))
  if (d$estimate == d$statistic) sprintf("every %s tank, %d of %d", lab, as.integer(d$estimate), as.integer(d$n))
  else sprintf("%s tanks, between %d and %d of %d", lab, as.integer(d$estimate), as.integer(d$statistic), as.integer(d$n))
}
```

```{r design-facts, include=FALSE}
# Facts quoted in the text that are not in output/paper/. Each is computed
# here from the processed data so the page cannot drift from the data.
`%>%` <- dplyr::`%>%`
and_list <- function(x) if (length(x) < 2) as.character(x) else
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))

# Heat ramp before Day 0 (heated tanks 4, 5, 10, 11; fixed plumbing).
apex_d <- readRDS(proc_file("apex_temperature_daily.rds")) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(tank = as.integer(sub("Temp", "", probe)))
heated_on <- function(d) mean(apex_d$value_mean[apex_d$tank %in% c(4, 5, 10, 11) &
                                                  apex_d$date == as.Date(d)])
ramp_start <- sprintf("%.1f", heated_on("2025-05-28"))
ramp_end   <- sprintf("%.1f", heated_on("2025-06-01"))

# Ambient tank 3 against the other ambient tanks, Days 0-15.
t_d015 <- apex_d %>% dplyr::filter(date >= as.Date("2025-06-04"), date <= as.Date("2025-06-19"))
t3_temp <- sprintf("%.1f", mean(t_d015$value_mean[t_d015$tank == 3]))
oth_temp <- sprintf("%.1f", range(tapply(t_d015$value_mean[t_d015$tank %in% c(6, 9, 12)],
                                         t_d015$tank[t_d015$tank %in% c(6, 9, 12)], mean)))
ysi_tank <- read.csv(table_file("09_ysi_tank_means.csv"))
t3_do <- sprintf("%.2f", ysi_tank$mean[ysi_tank$variable == "do_mgl" & ysi_tank$tank == 3])
oth_do <- sprintf("%.2f", range(ysi_tank$mean[ysi_tank$variable == "do_mgl" & ysi_tank$tank %in% c(6, 9, 12)]))

# Flatworms: daily morphology record (Day 15 fragments) and the worm survey of all 192.
physio <- readRDS(proc_file("physio_clean.rds"))
aef <- physio %>% dplyr::filter(disease_status %in% "AEF")
aef_ids <- unique(aef$id)
aef_checks <- nrow(aef)
aef_frags <- length(aef_ids)
aef_amb <- sum(aef$treatment == "28C")
aef_clipped <- dplyr::n_distinct(aef$id[aef$wound == "yes"])
aef_days <- and_list(sort(unique(aef$day)))
bud31 <- physio %>%
  dplyr::filter(wound == "yes", treatment == "31C") %>%
  dplyr::group_by(id) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(budded = any(new_corallites_on_tip %in% 1), .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(aef = id %in% aef_ids)
bud_noaef <- sum(bud31$budded & !bud31$aef); n_noaef <- sum(!bud31$aef)
bud_aef   <- sum(bud31$budded & bud31$aef);  n_aef   <- sum(bud31$aef)
worms <- readRDS(proc_file("worm_clean.rds"))
w_pos <- tapply(worms$present, worms$treatment, sum, na.rm = TRUE)
w_n   <- tapply(worms$present, worms$treatment, length)
w_dates <- dplyr::n_distinct(worms$date)

# Day 0 skeletal dry mass (plug removed), clipped vs unclipped.
bw <- readRDS(proc_file("buoyant_weight_clean.rds"))
bw0 <- tapply(bw$initial_dry, bw$wound, mean)
bw0_clip <- sprintf("%.2f", bw0[["yes"]]); bw0_unclip <- sprintf("%.2f", bw0[["no"]])

# Microscope experiment: Fisher's exact test of radial corallites by Day 15.
micro_fisher_p <- fisher.test(matrix(c(8, 0, 2, 6), 2, byrow = TRUE))$p.value

# Per-patch heat effects (ambient minus heated), Hochberg-adjusted p by clipping group.
patch_eff <- read.csv(table_file("12_genet_treatment_effects.csv"))
hochberg_c <- function(r) {
  x <- patch_eff[patch_eff$response == r & patch_eff$thicket == "c", ]
  sprintf("%s (unclipped) and %s (clipped)",
          fp(x$p_hochberg[x$wound == "no"]), fp(x$p_hochberg[x$wound == "yes"]))
}
zoox_fold <- function(p) sprintf("%.1f", exp(mean(patch_eff$estimate[
  patch_eff$response == "log_zoox_density" & patch_eff$thicket == p])))
zoox_loss <- function(p) sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (1 - 1 / exp(mean(patch_eff$estimate[
  patch_eff$response == "log_zoox_density" & patch_eff$thicket == p]))))

# Oxygen drop expected from warmer water alone at the same saturation.
do_expected <- sprintf("%.2f", pn("do_solubility_drop")$estimate)
do_observed <- sprintf("%.2f", pn("do_solubility_drop")$statistic)
```

<div class="banner">
<strong>What we found:</strong> After 15 days at 31 °C, coral fragments were paler, held fewer algal symbionts and gained less skeletal mass than fragments at 28 °C. Clipped fragments healed at both temperatures. But only 4 of 12 clipped fragments at 31 °C formed new radial corallites, the small skeletal cups on a regrown tip, by Day 15, against 12 of 12 at 28 °C. Heat changed fragments from source patch C less than those from A and D.<br>
<strong>How sure we are:</strong> We heated whole tanks, so we judged each heat effect by the four tanks at each temperature, not by the individual fragments. Paling, the drop in photosynthetic efficiency and the loss of symbionts are clear on that basis, and so is the stage 5 result: every ambient tank had 3 of 3 clipped fragments form radial corallites, every heated tank 1 of 3. The growth result is weaker, because one ambient tank grew about as little as the heated tanks. Each "Statistics" drop-down gives draft methods and results text.<br>
<strong>Genetics:</strong> We have final host clusters for the 144 fragments sampled on Days 1, 3 and 10, but none for the Day 15 fragments. A, C and D name field source patches, not genotypes. Our symbiont typing is rough.
</div>

## The experiment

We held fragments of *Acropora* cf. *pulchra* at 28 °C (ambient) or 31 °C (heated) and clipped about 1 cm off the growing tip of half of them, the standard cut used to make coral microfragments. Over 15 days we tracked healing and regeneration, skeletal growth, color, photosynthetic efficiency and the density of **algal symbionts**, the algae living in the coral tissue. *cf.* ("compare with") marks the species name as provisional until the taxonomy is settled.

- **Fragments:** 192 unbranched fragments about 6 cm tall, collected on 18–19 May 2025 from three field **source patches** (A, C and D). A source patch is where a fragment's parent branch grew; it is not a confirmed genotype.
- **Tanks:** eight tanks, four at each temperature. We raised the heated tanks from `r ramp_start` °C on 28 May to `r ramp_end` °C on 1 June and held them at 31 °C from then on, so heated fragments had three days at 31 °C before clipping.
- **Clipping:** on Day 0 (4 June) we clipped half the fragments in every tank. The unclipped fragments were sham-handled but not cut.
- **Sampling:** each tank held 24 fragments, one per source patch, clipping treatment and sampling day. We destructively sampled 48 fragments on each of Days 1, 3, 10 and 15 (192 in all). The 48 Day 15 fragments, 24 of them clipped, carry the repeated records: Fv/Fm, color, growth and daily regeneration scores.
- **Microscope experiment:** we ran a separate 16-fragment experiment to photograph healing under a dissecting microscope (details in section 3).

**Figure key.** Our figures carry no legends, so this key applies throughout. Temperature: <span class="t28">blue = 28 °C</span>, <span class="t31">orange = 31 °C</span>; where line type or symbol shape also marks temperature, 28 °C is solid with circles and 31 °C is dashed with triangles. Clipping: open symbols, white boxes and dashed lines = unclipped; filled symbols, gray boxes and solid lines = clipped (in the color-score figure, gray = unclipped and black = clipped; in the host-cluster symbiont figure, circles = unclipped and triangles = clipped). Source patches: gold = A, green = C, dark blue = D. Symbiont reference groups: green = S1, pink = S2, gold = S3, dark blue = S4. An X marks a fragment that had not reached a stage by Day 15.

## What we found

### 1. The 3 °C difference held

Every tank logged 144 readings a day, one every 10 minutes, from Day 0 through Day 15 (4–19 June 2025). Daily tank means averaged **27.78 °C** in the ambient tanks and **30.87 °C** in the heated tanks, a **3.09 °C difference**.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_apex}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("08_apex_temperature.png"))
```

**Water conditions.** We took handheld meter readings in all eight tanks on 14 dates from 5 to 19 June (none on 7 June), 112 readings in all.

```{r ysi-summary, echo=FALSE}
ysi_overall <- read.csv(here::here("output/tables/09_ysi_study_summary.csv"))
ysi_treatment <- read.csv(here::here("output/tables/09_ysi_treatment_summary.csv"))
ysi_vars <- c("sal", "do_mgl", "ph")
ysi_fmt <- function(d) {
  d <- d[match(ysi_vars, d$variable), ]
  sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", d$mean, d$sd_readings)
}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Measure=c("Salinity (unitless)", "Dissolved oxygen (mg/L)", "pH"),
  `All tanks`=ysi_fmt(ysi_overall),
  `28 °C`=ysi_fmt(subset(ysi_treatment, treatment == "28C")),
  `31 °C`=ysi_fmt(subset(ysi_treatment, treatment == "31C")),
  check.names=FALSE), row.names=FALSE)
```

Values are means ± standard deviations across readings; each temperature has four tanks and 56 readings, and repeat readings from a tank are not extra replicates. The meter did not record which pH scale it used.

Salinity and pH barely moved. Heated tanks held less dissolved oxygen (`r est("ysi_do_heated")` vs `r est("ysi_do_ambient")` mg/L). Warmer water holds less oxygen, but that accounts for only about `r do_expected` mg/L of the `r do_observed` mg/L drop; the rest came from slightly lower saturation in heated tanks (`r est("ysi_do_pct_heated", 0)`% vs `r est("ysi_do_pct_ambient", 0)`%). Both were above 100%, so the corals were not short of oxygen when we measured, but spot checks cannot rule out changes between visits, and we cannot separate the effects of heat from those of lower oxygen.

```{r, fig.cap="Water conditions from a handheld YSI meter, 4–19 June 2025. Each line follows one tank; blue = 28 °C and orange = 31 °C, four tanks per temperature. Points are individual readings, and panels have different vertical scales. We converted temperature from Fahrenheit to Celsius; dissolved oxygen is in mg/L, and salinity and pH are unitless. We measured every tank on 14 dates and have no readings for 4 or 7 June; connecting lines do not stand for measurements on those dates."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("09_ysi_water_chem.png"))
```

<details class="stats">
<summary>Statistics: methods and results for tank temperature and water quality</summary>

##### What we measured
Water temperature in all eight tanks every 10 minutes from Day 0 (June 4) to Day 15 (June 19). Salinity, dissolved oxygen and pH with a handheld meter, once per tank on `r round(pn("ysi_sal")$df1)` of those 16 days (none on June 4 or 7), for `r nn("ysi_sal")` readings.

##### Methods text (draft)
<div class="ms">An Apex controller (Neptune Systems) recorded water temperature in each tank every 10 min. We raised the four heated tanks from 28 °C to 31 °C over four days (May 28–31, 2025) and held them at 31 °C from June 1; the four ambient tanks stayed at 28 °C. We averaged the readings for each tank on each day, then averaged those daily values across the four tanks in each treatment. We report Days 0–15, the period after clipping; the heated fragments had already spent three days at 31 °C before Day 0. We measured salinity, dissolved oxygen and pH with a handheld YSI ProQuatro multiparameter meter, once in each of the eight tanks on `r round(pn("ysi_sal")$df1)` days from June 5 to 19, 2025 (no readings on June 7). [VERIFY: how the Apex probes were checked against a reference thermometer; time of day of the YSI readings; pH scale.]</div>

##### Results text (draft)
<div class="ms">Ambient tanks averaged `r est("temp_mean_ambient")` °C and heated tanks `r est("temp_mean_heated")` °C, a difference of `r est("temp_difference")` °C. Daily means for single tanks ranged from `r sprintf("%.2f", pn("temp_mean_ambient")$ci_low)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", pn("temp_mean_ambient")$ci_high)` °C in ambient tanks and from `r sprintf("%.2f", pn("temp_mean_heated")$ci_low)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", pn("temp_mean_heated")$ci_high)` °C in heated tanks. Across all `r nn("ysi_sal")` meter readings (mean ± SD across tanks and days), salinity was `r sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", pn("ysi_sal")$estimate, pn("ysi_sal")$statistic)`, dissolved oxygen `r sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", pn("ysi_do_mgl")$estimate, pn("ysi_do_mgl")$statistic)` mg/L, and pH `r sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", pn("ysi_ph")$estimate, pn("ysi_ph")$statistic)`. Dissolved oxygen was lower in heated tanks (`r sprintf("%.2f", pn("ysi_do_heated")$estimate)` vs `r sprintf("%.2f", pn("ysi_do_ambient")$estimate)` mg/L). Warmer water alone would explain a drop of about `r do_expected` mg/L at the same saturation; the observed drop was `r do_observed` mg/L, because saturation was also a little lower in heated tanks (`r est("ysi_do_pct_heated", 0)`% vs `r est("ysi_do_pct_ambient", 0)`%). Both treatments were above 100% saturation. Because oxygen fell with temperature, our design cannot separate the effects of heat from those of lower oxygen.</div>

</details>

### 2. Heat lowered coral condition and growth

We use **coral condition** for three measures: photosynthetic efficiency (**Fv/Fm**, how efficiently the symbionts use light), tissue color, and symbiont density. At 31 °C all three fell over the two weeks, and heated fragments also gained less skeletal mass.

- Fv/Fm and color declined over time in heated fragments.
- Symbiont density dropped sharply over the two weeks.
- Heated fragments laid down **`r est("growth_pct_lower", 0)`% less** skeleton: their dry mass rose `r est("growth_heated", 1)`% over 15 days, against `r est("growth_ambient", 1)`% at 28 °C.

We treat the growth result as moderate evidence. One ambient tank, tank 3, grew about as little as the heated tanks, and we don't know why: it held `r t3_temp` °C (other ambient tanks `r oth_temp[1]`–`r oth_temp[2]` °C) and had similar oxygen (`r t3_do` mg/L vs `r oth_do[1]`–`r oth_do[2]`). With tank 3 included, the tank-level model test gives `r fp(pn("growth_temp")$p_value)`, and a stricter test that uses only the eight tank averages gives `r fp(pn("growth_tank_permutation")$p_value)`. Without tank 3, `r sens_p("growth", "without ambient tank 3")`; leaving out tank 12 instead gives `r sens_p("growth", "leave one tank out: highest p")`.

Cutting the tip did not make heat stress worse. Clipped and unclipped fragments paled and lost photosynthetic efficiency at about the same rate, and grew about the same. With 12 fragments per group, we could still miss a small effect. Under heat, clipped fragments kept *more* symbionts than unclipped ones, not fewer, but that difference depends on which tanks we include.

We averaged tip and base readings within each fragment, then averaged the four tank means per temperature and clipping group; bars show one standard error among tank means. B compares different fragments sampled on Days 1, 3, 10 and 15, 12 per temperature × clipping group per day (192 in total). C shows percent skeletal mass gain over 15 days in 48 fragments, 12 per group. In B and C, dots are fragments; boxes show the median and middle half, with whiskers to the most extreme values within 1.5 box lengths. Source patches are pooled for display but kept in the models. Day 0 marks clipping. Heated tanks reached 31 °C on 1 June, so Day −1 (3 June) is not an unheated baseline."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("45_physiology_figure2.png"))

<details class="stats">
<summary>Statistics: methods and results for photosynthesis, color, symbionts and growth</summary>

##### What we measured
- **Fv/Fm:** measured with a pulse-amplitude-modulated (PAM) fluorometer on dark-adapted fragments. We took two readings per fragment (near the tip and near the base) and averaged them. Same 48 fragments on Days −1, 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 and 14.
- **Color:** CoralWatch color-card score from 1 (palest) to 6 (darkest), same 48 fragments, Days −4 to 14.
- **Symbiont density:** we cut a tissue biopsy from each fragment with a band saw, removed the tissue with an airbrush, counted symbionts on a hemocytometer and measured the biopsy's surface area by wax dipping. Density is therefore per cm² of the sampled piece, not of the whole fragment, so a shorter clipped fragment does not change it. 12 fragments per temperature × clipping group per day (Days 1, 3, 10, 15), 192 in total.
- **Growth:** percent change in skeletal dry mass from Day 0 to Day 15, same 48 fragments. We calculated dry mass from buoyant weight (Davies 1989), measured seawater density with a glass reference object at each weighing, and subtracted the aragonite plug each fragment was glued to. Molly's Day 0 plan lists clipping before weighing, so growth runs from the clipped fragment. Day 0 dry mass was similar in clipped and unclipped fragments (`r bw0_clip` vs `r bw0_unclip` g), consistent with that order.

##### Methods text (draft)
<div class="ms">We analyzed Fv/Fm and color score with linear mixed models of Days 0–14. The readings taken before clipping (Day −1 for Fv/Fm, Day −4 for color) appear in the figures but not in the models. Fixed effects were temperature, clipping, day and source patch, with all their interactions; the full set lets one model test whether clipping or source patch changed the effect of heat over time. Day entered as a linear trend, so the temperature × day term tests whether heated fragments declined faster than ambient ones. Color is the CoralWatch D-scale score (1 = palest, 6 = darkest); a fragment scored between two cards (for example D3/D4) took the midpoint, and we analyzed the score as continuous. Because we applied temperature to whole tanks and measured fragments repeatedly, each model allowed each tank its own starting value and its own rate of change over time (a random intercept and day slope), and each fragment its own starting value. Giving each tank its own slope means the test of temperature × day compares tanks, not fragments. We analyzed symbiont density on a log scale, because treatment effects were proportional and the spread grew with the mean, with the same fixed effects and a random intercept and day slope for each tank; we sampled each fragment once. We analyzed growth with temperature, clipping, source patch and their interactions, and a random intercept for tank, so the temperature test for growth also compares tanks (4 per temperature). We fitted models with lme4 2.1-0 and lmerTest 3.2-1 in R 4.6.2 and used Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, an adjustment suited to small numbers of tanks. We checked residuals of every model with simulation-based diagnostics (DHARMa). Because the growth test rests on only four tanks per temperature, we also compared the four ambient and four heated tank means against all 70 possible ways of assigning four tanks to each treatment (an exact permutation test).</div>

##### Results text (draft)
<div class="ms">Fv/Fm declined faster in heated than in ambient fragments (temperature × day, `r fF("pam_temp_x_day")`). On Day 14, observed means were `r est("pam_day14_heated")` in heated and `r est("pam_day14_ambient")` in ambient fragments. The decline did not detectably differ between clipped and unclipped fragments (temperature × clipping × day, `r fF("pam_temp_x_wound_x_day")`).

Heated fragments also became paler faster (temperature × day, `r fF("color_temp_x_day")`). On the last day they averaged `r est("color_final_heated", 1)` on the 1–6 color card, compared with `r est("color_final_ambient", 1)` for ambient fragments. Again, the change did not detectably differ between clipped and unclipped fragments (temperature × clipping × day, `r fF("color_temp_x_wound_x_day")`).

Symbiont density fell faster in heated fragments (temperature × day, `r fF("zoox_temp_x_day")`). On Day 15, heated fragments held `r est("zoox_day15_heated")` million cells per cm², compared with `r est("zoox_day15_ambient")` million in ambient fragments. Clipping did not detectably change this decline (temperature × clipping × day, `r fF("zoox_temp_x_wound_x_day")`). If anything, heated clipped fragments kept more symbionts than heated unclipped ones: `r est("zoox_heated_wound_ratio_day10")` times as many on Day 10 and `r est("zoox_heated_wound_ratio_day15")` times as many on Day 15, with more in clipped fragments on both days in `r cnt("zoox_heated_tanks_wounded_higher")` of `r nn("zoox_heated_tanks_wounded_higher")` heated tanks. This difference depends on which tanks we include: leaving out one tank at a time moves the *p* value from `r sub("\\*p\\* = ", "", sens_p("symbionts", "leave one tank out: lowest p"))` to `r sub("\\*p\\* = ", "", sens_p("symbionts", "leave one tank out: highest p"))`.

Heated fragments grew `r est("growth_pct_lower", 0)`% less than ambient fragments (`r est("growth_heated", 1)`% vs `r est("growth_ambient", 1)`% gain in skeletal mass over 15 days; temperature, `r fF("growth_temp")`). The exact permutation test of tank means gave `r fp(pn("growth_tank_permutation")$p_value)`, and the test depends on which tanks are included: ambient tank 3 grew about as little as the heated tanks, and leaving it out gives `r sens_p("growth", "without ambient tank 3")`, while leaving out tank 12 instead gives `r sens_p("growth", "leave one tank out: highest p")`. We therefore treat the growth effect as moderate evidence. Clipping did not detectably change growth (clipping, `r fF("growth_wound", 2)`; temperature × clipping, `r fF("growth_temp_x_wound", 2)`).</div>

<div class="dont">

**Growth test:** the model test is the main result; the tank permutation (`r fp(pn("growth_tank_permutation")$p_value)`) and the tank 3 check go in the text as a caveat, with full details in the supplement. Both tests point the same way, but only the model test is below 0.05, so we call the growth effect moderate evidence.

**Wording:** "no difference between clipped and unclipped" means we found no evidence of one with 12 fragments per group. It does not show that clipping has no effect.

</div>

</details>

### 3. Clipped fragments healed, but heat blocked the last regeneration stage

We split recovery from clipping into **healing** and **regeneration**:

- **Healing:** the coenosarc, the sheet of living tissue between polyps, covers the wound.
- **Regeneration**, five stages scored daily in the main experiment:
  1. the axial polyp (the polyp at the branch tip) forms in the wound;
  2. the wound surface remodels (smooths over);
  3. the axial corallite, the new tip, forms;
  4. the axial corallite extends;
  5. new radial corallites, the side cups, form on the new tip.

Tissue covered the wound within a day at both temperatures, and nearly every fragment reached regeneration stages 1–4. Stage 5 differed. By Day 15, **12 of 12 ambient** fragments had formed new radial corallites, against **4 of 12 heated** fragments. The split was the same in every tank: three of three clipped fragments in each ambient tank, one of three in each heated tank. Our 15-day experiment cannot tell whether the heated fragments would have reached stage 5 later.

The separate microscope experiment repeated the result. There, `r cnt("micro_budding_day15_ambient")` of 8 ambient and `r cnt("micro_budding_day15_heated")` of 8 heated fragments formed new radial corallites by Day 15. This experiment used 16 other fragments from patches A and C, in four other tanks (two at each temperature, four fragments per tank), about a month later. We collected them on 17 June, raised two tanks to 31 °C over 27–29 June, clipped all 16 on 5 July and photographed them daily until 20 July. It is the only experiment that recorded when tissue first covered the wound.

```{r, fig.cap=cap_stage_cumulative}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("39d_stage_cumulative_all_stages.png"))
```

Figure 1B in the manuscript shows four of these panels: regeneration stages 1, 3, 4 and 5. Stage 2 goes in the supplement.

The gap opened before Day 15. By Day 8, `r frac("tip_extension_pct_day8_ambient")` ambient fragments had an extending axial corallite (stage 4), against `r frac("tip_extension_pct_day8_heated")` heated fragments. By Day 12, `r frac("budding_pct_day12_ambient")` ambient fragments had new radial corallites, against `r frac("budding_pct_day12_heated")` heated fragments.

**Flatworms do not explain the stage 5 result.** Acropora-eating flatworms appeared mostly in heated tanks. In the daily record of the 48 Day 15 fragments, we noted flatworm signs `r aef_checks` times, on `r aef_frags` heated fragments (`r aef_clipped` of them clipped), on Days `r aef_days`, around the Day 4 treatment dip. We noted none on ambient fragments. A separate survey of all 192 fragments on `r w_dates` dates found worms on `r w_pos[["31C"]]` heated and `r w_pos[["28C"]]` ambient fragment checks. Among heated clipped fragments with no flatworm record, `r bud_noaef` of `r n_noaef` formed new radial corallites, about the same as the `r bud_aef` of `r n_aef` with a record. Flatworms were therefore a second difference between the temperatures, but the heated fragments without them still fell far short of 12 of 12.

**How we counted.** The curves and the table below count a fragment once we first saw it at a stage, and keep counting it even if a later score marks the feature absent. A later absence could be a real change or a scoring slip, and we do not try to separate the two. The stages also need not follow a fixed order: a fragment can form radial corallites in the wound area before its axial corallite visibly extends.

```{r}
stage_summary_tbl <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path("..", "..", "output", "tables", "36_stage_timing_mean_iqr.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
stage_names <- c("Healing: tissue covers wound", "1. Axial polyp forms",
                 "2. Wound surface remodels", "3. Axial corallite forms",
                 "4. Axial corallite extends", "5. Radial corallites form")
attainment <- stage_summary_tbl |>
  dplyr::mutate(Stage = stage_names[stage_order],
                value = sprintf("%d/%d (%.0f%%)", n_reached, n_scored, pct_reached)) |>
  dplyr::select(Stage, treatment, value) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = treatment, values_from = value)
knitr::kable(attainment, caption = paste(
  "Clipped fragments we saw at each stage at least once by Day 15.",
  "Healing comes from the microscope experiment; regeneration stages come from the main experiment."
))
```

**Average time to each stage.** We give average first-observation days only for stages every fragment reached at both temperatures. For the others, an average would describe only the fragments that got there.

```{r}
complete_timing <- stage_summary_tbl |>
  dplyr::filter(complete_both_temperatures) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Stage = stage_names[stage_order], Temperature = treatment,
                   `Mean first-observation day` = mean_day,
                   `Middle half of first days` = iqr_days)
knitr::kable(complete_timing, digits = 2, caption = paste(
  "Timing for stages every fragment reached at both temperatures.",
  "The middle-half range runs from the 25th to the 75th percentile.",
  "These are the days we first saw each stage, not exact biological onset times."
))
```

```{r, fig.cap=cap_molly_stage_violin}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("36b_stage_violin.png"))
```

<summary>Exact observation days for each fragment</summary>

```{r, fig.cap=cap_molly_stage_timing}

We scored pigment over the wound only on Days 3, 4, 9, 12 and 15, so we don't know about the other days. Pigment is not one of the stages, and so few scores support only a rough timing comparison.

<details>
<summary>Other daily observations (polyps, pigment, algae, flatworms)</summary>

```{r, fig.cap=cap_other_obs}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("47_other_daily_observations.png"))
```

</details>

**Fewer, not later.** Within our 15 days, heat mainly cut how many fragments formed radial corallites, rather than pushing them a few days later: 8 of 12 heated fragments had none by Day 15. The four heated fragments that did form them did so on Days `r cnt("budding_first_day_range_heated")`–`r cnt("budding_first_day_range_heated", "statistic")`, the same window as ambient fragments (Days `r cnt("budding_first_day_range_ambient")`–`r cnt("budding_first_day_range_ambient", "statistic")`). A timing model that counts the eight as "not yet" estimates that stage 5 took `r est("new_corallites_on_tip_time_ratio")` times as long at 31 °C, but that number mostly reflects the fragments that had none by Day 15. Whether they would have formed them with more time is an open question (below). The axial corallite extended on a similar schedule at both temperatures.

A healed wound is not a regenerated tip. Had we scored only healing, we would have missed the main heat effect.

```

cat(vid("morphology_ambient_healing.mp4",

<details class="stats">
<summary>Statistics: methods and results for healing and regeneration</summary>

##### What we measured
**Main experiment:** we scored the 24 clipped fragments among the 48 followed to Day 15 (12 per temperature) every day from Day 0 to Day 15, recording whether each of the five regeneration stages was present.

**Microscope experiment:** we photographed 16 other clipped fragments (8 per temperature, patches A and C, two tanks per temperature) daily under a dissecting microscope from July 5 to 20, 2025, and scored healing and the regeneration stages from the photos. Because it used different fragments, tanks and dates, we analyzed it separately.

##### Methods text (draft)
<div class="ms">We scored each clipped fragment once a day [VERIFY: scored live or from photos, and whether the scorer knew each fragment's temperature] and recorded the first day we saw each stage. We compared the number of fragments showing each stage on Day 15 between temperatures with Fisher's exact tests; we used presence on Day 15, rather than ever reaching the stage, because it is the fragment's state at the end of the experiment (the two counts differ by one fragment, for stage 4 only). To compare how long fragments took to reach a stage, we used time-to-event models. Because we scored fragments once a day, each stage began at some point between the last check without it and the first check with it. Interval-censored log-logistic models use that interval rather than assuming the stage began exactly on the day we first saw it. Among Weibull, lognormal, log-logistic and exponential models, the log-logistic fitted best, or within 0.6 AIC units of the best, for every stage. We kept fragments that had not reached a stage by Day 15 in the analysis as "not yet reached" rather than dropping them. The time-to-event models included source patch. We checked them with Cox proportional-hazards models stratified by source patch and with log-rank tests on the first day we saw each stage (survival 3.8-12 in R 4.6.2). Because we applied temperature to whole tanks, we also report the outcome for each tank and an exact permutation test comparing the proportion of clipped fragments in each tank that formed radial corallites between the four ambient and four heated tanks. In the separate microscope experiment, we compared the number of fragments that formed radial corallites by Day 15 between temperatures with a Fisher's exact test; it had only two tanks per temperature, too few for a tank-level test.</div>

##### Results text (draft)
<div class="ms">In the microscope experiment, tissue covered the wound by Day 1 in all `r cnt("tissue_cover_by_day1")` of `r nn("tissue_cover_by_day1")` fragments at both temperatures. In the main experiment, every fragment at both temperatures formed an axial polyp (`r cnt("axial_polyp_formation_reached_by_day15")` of `r nn("axial_polyp_formation_reached_by_day15")` ambient, `r cnt("axial_polyp_formation_reached_by_day15", "statistic")` of `r nn("axial_polyp_formation_reached_by_day15")` heated) and remodeled the wound surface (`r cnt("wound_smoothed_reached_by_day15")` of 12, `r cnt("wound_smoothed_reached_by_day15", "statistic")` of 12), and `r cnt("tip_exist_reached_by_day15")` of 12 at each temperature formed a new axial corallite. Heat detectably affected only the last stage. By Day 15, `r cnt("new_corallites_on_tip_reached_by_day15")` of 12 ambient fragments had formed new radial corallites, compared with `r cnt("new_corallites_on_tip_reached_by_day15", "statistic")` of 12 heated fragments (Fisher's exact test, `r fp(pn("new_corallites_on_tip_present_day15")$p_value)`). The pattern held tank by tank: in `r tank_txt("ambient")` clipped fragments formed radial corallites; in `r tank_txt("heated")` did (exact tank permutation, `r fp(pn("budding_tank_permutation")$p_value)`, the smallest value possible with four tanks per temperature). Most heated fragments never formed them in the 15 days, so the effect is mainly in how many fragments got there. Treating the `r 12 - as.integer(pn("new_corallites_on_tip_reached_by_day15")$statistic)` heated fragments without radial corallites as "not yet by Day 15", a time-to-event model estimated that the stage took about `r est("new_corallites_on_tip_time_ratio", 1)` times as long under heat (time ratio `r fci("new_corallites_on_tip_time_ratio")`). On any given day, heated fragments were about one-fifth as likely as ambient fragments to form them (Cox hazard ratio `r fci("budding_hazard_ratio")`). The axial corallite extended in `r cnt("tip_extension_reached_by_day15")` of 12 ambient and `r cnt("tip_extension_reached_by_day15", "statistic")` of 12 heated fragments, and the timing did not detectably differ between temperatures (time ratio `r fci("tip_extension_time_ratio")`). Flatworms, which we recorded only on heated fragments, do not explain the stage 5 result: among heated clipped fragments with no flatworm record, `r bud_noaef` of `r n_noaef` formed new radial corallites. In the microscope experiment, `r cnt("micro_budding_day15_ambient")` of 8 ambient and `r cnt("micro_budding_day15_heated")` of 8 heated fragments formed new radial corallites by Day 15 (Fisher's exact test, `r fp(micro_fisher_p)`; two tanks per temperature).</div>

<div class="dont">

**Fragments 115 and 121:** 121 was scored with radial corallites on Day 15 but no axial corallite that day, and 115 formed radial corallites on Day 14, before its axial corallite extended on Day 15. Without both fragments the result is 11 of 11 ambient vs 3 of 11 heated, so it does not depend on them.

**Two counts for stage 4:** the Fisher tests count a stage only if it was still visible on Day 15, which gives `r cnt("tip_extension_present_day15")` vs `r cnt("tip_extension_present_day15", "statistic")` fragments for an extending axial corallite. The table above counts any fragment seen at the stage by Day 15, which gives `r cnt("tip_extension_reached_by_day15")` vs `r cnt("tip_extension_reached_by_day15", "statistic")`. The difference is one heated fragment whose extension was scored and later not.

**Tanks:** the timing models, the Cox model and the Fisher and log-rank tests treat each fragment as independent, but three clipped fragments shared each tank. We use the time ratio and hazard ratio as effect sizes, and cite the per-tank counts and the tank permutation for significance.

**What we don't report:**

- *p*-values from daily yes/no models of each stage. Their results shifted with the computer and package versions.
- the average day a stage was reached, for stages some fragments never reached. For stage 5 under heat, that average would describe only 4 of 12 fragments.

**Source patches:** every ambient fragment formed radial corallites, but under heat the count differed by source patch: `r cnt("budding_heated_patch_A")` of `r nn("budding_heated_patch_A")` from patch A, `r cnt("budding_heated_patch_C")` of `r nn("budding_heated_patch_C")` from C and `r cnt("budding_heated_patch_D")` of `r nn("budding_heated_patch_D")` from D. With four fragments per group, and none at all from heated patch A, the Cox source patch × temperature test is unreliable, so we report these counts instead of its *p*-value. We treat this as a lead to follow up, not a result.

</div>

</details>

### 4. Heat changed source patch C less

Under heat, fragments from **source patch C** lost less Fv/Fm, color and symbiont density than fragments from A and D. Growth differed among patches in another way: patch C grew less than A and D at 28 °C, and all three grew about the same at 31 °C. So C's smaller heat effect on growth comes from slow growth at 28 °C, not better growth at 31 °C.

We compare each patch at 31 °C with the same patch at 28 °C, which measures how much heat changed each patch, not which patch started highest. By Day 14, heat lowered Fv/Fm by `r est("heat_drop_pam_fvfm_patch_C", 2)` in patch C, against `r est("heat_drop_pam_fvfm_patch_D", 2)`–`r est("heat_drop_pam_fvfm_patch_A", 2)` in A and D, and lowered color by `r est("heat_drop_color_dscale_patch_C", 1)` card points, against `r est("heat_drop_color_dscale_patch_D", 1)`–`r est("heat_drop_color_dscale_patch_A", 1)`. By Day 15, heated patch C fragments held about `r zoox_loss("c")`% fewer symbionts than ambient patch C fragments, against about `r zoox_loss("d")`% fewer in D and `r zoox_loss("a")`% fewer in A.

```{r, fig.cap="Heat lowered every measure less in source patch C. Each panel shows end-of-experiment means for patches A, C and D: Fv/Fm and color on Day 14, symbiont density on Day 15 (log scale) and growth over Days 0–15. Patches A, C and D are gold, green and dark blue. Bars show one standard error across fragments (8 per patch and temperature), not tank-level uncertainty. Lines that are not parallel mean the heat effect differs among patches. These are raw means; the formal tests are in the Statistics drop-down below."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("13_genet_response_panel.png"))
```

<details class="stats">
<summary>Statistics: methods and results for source-patch differences</summary>

##### What we measured
The same measures as above, split by source patch. Each patch contributed 16 of the 48 fragments followed to Day 15, split evenly across temperatures and clipping.

##### Methods text (draft)
<div class="ms">The three source patches could hold different genotypes, so we tested whether the effect of heat differed among them [VERIFY: whether this test was planned before the data came in]. For each measure, we compared the full model with one that dropped the source patch × temperature term and all its higher-order interactions (with clipping and day), using a likelihood-ratio test. For Fv/Fm, color and symbiont density this removes eight terms, and for growth four, which sets the degrees of freedom of each test. We then estimated the ambient-minus-heated difference for each patch and clipping group from the full model: on Day 14 for Fv/Fm and color, on Day 15 for symbiont density, and over Days 0–15 for growth. Each measure has six such differences (three patches × two clipping groups), so we adjusted their *p* values for multiple tests with the Hochberg method.</div>

##### Results text (draft)
<div class="ms">The effect of heat differed among source patches for Fv/Fm (`r fchi("patch_x_temp_pam_fvfm")`), color (`r fchi("patch_x_temp_color_dscale")`) and symbiont density (`r fchi("patch_x_temp_log_zoox")`). The temperature effect on growth also differed among patches (`r fchi("patch_x_temp_growth_pct")`), because patch C grew less than A and D at 28 °C; at 31 °C the three patches grew similarly. The heat effect was smallest in patch C for all three condition measures. By Day 14, heat lowered Fv/Fm by `r est("heat_drop_pam_fvfm_patch_C", 3)` in patch C, compared with `r est("heat_drop_pam_fvfm_patch_A", 3)` in A and `r est("heat_drop_pam_fvfm_patch_D", 3)` in D (model estimates averaged over clipping). Color fell by `r est("heat_drop_color_dscale_patch_C", 1)` points on the 1–6 card in C, compared with `r est("heat_drop_color_dscale_patch_A", 1)` in A and `r est("heat_drop_color_dscale_patch_D", 1)` in D. On Day 15, ambient fragments held about `r zoox_fold("c")` times as many symbionts as heated fragments in patch C, compared with `r zoox_fold("a")` times in A and `r zoox_fold("d")` times in D. The patch C differences are the least certain: Hochberg-adjusted *p* values for the heat effect in C were `r hochberg_c("pam_fvfm")` for Fv/Fm, and `r hochberg_c("color_dscale")` for color. All 48 sequenced patch C fragments fell in one host cluster, and patch C came from one spot on the reef, so its smaller heat effect could reflect genotype, collection site or symbionts; these data cannot separate them.</div>

<div class="dont">

**Source patches vs genotypes:** source patches are field labels, not confirmed genotypes. Rachael's host clusters put all 48 sequenced patch C fragments in one cluster, while A and D each contain several.

**Per-patch heat effects:** we tested six contrasts per measure (three patches × two clipping groups) and adjusted the *p*-values for multiple tests (Hochberg method). The patch C estimates are the smallest and least certain.

**What this can show:** with three patches, we can describe differences among these patches. We cannot estimate how much heat tolerance varies among genotypes in the wider population.

</div>

</details>

### 5. Host clusters and their symbionts

Rachael's lab grouped our fragments by genetic similarity using **single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)**, differences at single DNA positions, read from the RNA sequencing data. We call each group a **host cluster**. The fragments fall into eight host clusters. The assignments cover only the 144 sequenced fragments; they do not carry over automatically to other fragments from the same source patch.

- All **48 fragments from C** fall in cluster 1.
- The 48 fragments from A fall in clusters 4, 5, 6 and 7, mostly cluster 4.
- The 48 fragments from D fall in clusters 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8.
- A and D share clusters 4 and 5.

```{r, fig.cap="The sequenced fragments fall into eight host clusters, and patch C forms one of them. Left: each point is one of 144 sequenced fragments, placed on the first two principal components of the SNP data. Source patches A, C and D are gold, green and dark blue. Right: the number of fragments in each cluster, split by source patch; labels mark the larger segments. Cluster sizes are 48, 17, 16, 52, 7, 2, 1 and 1. Host clusters and source patches are different groupings."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("43_final_snp_structure.png"))
```

We assigned treatments by source patch before we had genetic results, so the clusters are unevenly spread across treatments.

```{r, fig.cap="Host clusters are unevenly spread across treatments. Each tile gives the number of sequenced fragments for a host cluster, temperature, sampling day and clipping treatment. A zero means an empty combination, not a missing genetic assignment. Clusters 7 and 8 have only heated fragments, and cluster 6 has one fragment per temperature. These clusters are too small to compare heat responses."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("43_final_snp_design.png"))
```

**Which measures can we link to host clusters?** We sampled the 144 sequenced fragments on Days 1, 3 and 10. Symbiont density is the only measure we took on those same fragments, so it is the only one we can link directly to host clusters. The 48 Day 15 fragments carry the fuller record (Fv/Fm, color, growth and regeneration), but they have not been sequenced. We plan to move ahead with the existing samples rather than hold the paper for new sequencing.

```{r, fig.cap="Symbiont density within host clusters. Each point is one fragment; blue = 28 °C and orange = 31 °C; circles = unclipped and triangles = clipped. Sampling days stay separate rather than pooled. The vertical axis is millions of algal cells per square centimeter on a log scale, so equal spacing means equal fold change. Small horizontal offsets separate overlapping points. These are raw observations, not adjusted treatment estimates."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("43_final_snp_symbiont_density.png"))
```

Cluster 1, which holds all the patch C fragments, lost fewer symbionts under heat than clusters 2–4. That holds after accounting for tank, sampling day and clipping, and when we leave out fragments dominated by symbionts other than S1. It is the same density data grouped by genotype instead of by patch, so it is not independent evidence that genotype controls the response. The clusters are small and uneven and the model fits imperfectly, so we treat these comparisons as exploratory; we show clusters 6–8 but leave them out of the model.

**Which symbionts dominate?** Rachael's lab also mapped sequence reads, short pieces of sequence, to four reference symbiont genomes. We call these **reference groups S1–S4** (Rachael's labels A–D, renamed here so they don't collide with our source-patch letters). The share of reads mapping to each reference gives a rough picture of each fragment's symbiont mix. S1, identified as *Symbiodinium*, dominates **138 of 144 fragments**. S4 dominates five and S3 one.

```{r, fig.cap="Rough symbiont typing from sequence-read mapping. Each bar is a fragment; green, pink, gold and dark blue portions show the shares of reads mapping to reference groups S1, S2, S3 and S4, which sum to one. Panels are host clusters 1–8, with 48, 17, 16, 52, 7, 2, 1 and 1 fragments, so bar widths differ among panels. Fragments are ordered by their S1 share, not by time. These shares are not cell proportions or symbiont density, and a dominant group does not mean no other group is present."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig("43_final_snp_symbiont_typing.png"))
```

All six fragments not dominated by S1 were heated and clipped; we sampled five on Day 10 and one on Day 1. We cannot tell whether heat shifted their symbiont mix or whether they differed from the start. That makes the mix worth checking in the expression analyses, but it is not evidence that symbiont type drove the heat response.

## Take-homes

- **The 3 °C difference held.** All eight tanks have a complete temperature record through Day 15 (mean difference 3.09 °C). Heated tanks held less oxygen, partly because warm water holds less, and we cannot separate heat from lower oxygen.
- **Heat lowered coral condition.** Over two weeks at 31 °C, fragments paled, their symbionts used light less efficiently (lower Fv/Fm), and they lost most of their symbionts. These effects are clear even when each tank counts as a single replicate.
- **Heated fragments laid down `r est("growth_pct_lower", 0)`% less skeleton**, but that result is weaker because it depends on one ambient tank that grew little.
- **Cutting the tip did not make heat stress worse.** Clipped and unclipped fragments declined at about the same rate. If anything, clipped heated fragments kept *more* symbionts, not fewer.
- **Heat blocked the last regeneration stage, not healing.** Tissue covered the wound within a day at both temperatures, and nearly every fragment reached regeneration stages 1–4. New radial corallites formed in 12 of 12 ambient versus 4 of 12 heated fragments by Day 15, in every tank, and the microscope experiment repeated it (`r cnt("micro_budding_day15_ambient")` of 8 vs `r cnt("micro_budding_day15_heated")` of 8). Flatworms do not explain it.
- **Heat changed source patch C least.** Heat lowered Fv/Fm, color and symbiont density less in C than in A or D. All 48 sequenced fragments from C belong to one host cluster, so we cannot separate patch from genotype for C.
- **The design limits what the genetic and symbiont data can show.** We have host clusters only for the 144 fragments sampled on Days 1, 3 and 10, and they are unevenly spread across treatments. Most fragments carry mainly S1 symbionts; the six exceptions were all heated and clipped.

## Open questions

- **Was stage 5 delayed or blocked?** Partly answered. At 28 °C, the `r nn("bud_lag_ambient")` fragments with both events recorded formed radial corallites `r est("bud_lag_ambient", 0)` to `r cnt("bud_lag_ambient", "statistic")` days after their axial corallite began to extend; the twelfth did so on Day 15 with no extension recorded. At 31 °C, `r cnt("bud_stalled_heated")` of 12 fragments had an extending axial corallite for longer than that and still had no radial corallites by Day 15. The last heated fragment to form them did so on Day `r cnt("budding_first_day_range_heated", "statistic")`. Heat therefore slowed or stalled the step from extension to radial corallites, but we cannot separate a long delay from a permanent block. Whether those fragments would recover with more time, or after a return to 28 °C, needs a longer experiment.
- **What makes patch C more tolerant?** Not yet known. One lead: patch C carried a second symbiont group alongside S1. At 28 °C, `r cnt("sym_D_over5pct_28C_patch_C")` of 24 patch C fragments had more than 5% of their symbiont reads in S4, against `r cnt("sym_D_over5pct_28C_patch_A")` of 24 from patch A and `r cnt("sym_D_over5pct_28C_patch_D")` of 24 from patch D. We don't know what S4 is; Rachael has confirmed only that S1 is *Symbiodinium*. If S4 proves to be *Durusdinium*, a genus often linked to heat tolerance, that would fit, but for now it is a question for Rachael, not a finding. Patch C is a single host cluster from one field patch, so host genotype, symbionts and field history travel together. Separating them would take patch C hosts with and without S4, or more genotypes per patch.
- **Which gene responses go with slower regeneration?** We can't answer this yet. The expression counts haven't arrived; Rachael and Shreya are rerunning the processing. We chose the expression days (1, 3 and 10) before the experiment, to catch the first-day wound response and the days after it. Radial corallites then formed on Days 12–15, after the last expression sample, and the sequenced fragments were destroyed when we sampled them. Expression can therefore test group differences (heat, clipping, and whether patch C responds differently), but it cannot link one fragment's genes to that fragment's regeneration.
- **Did lower oxygen in the heated tanks contribute?** We cannot fully separate oxygen from temperature. Heated tanks averaged `r est("ysi_do_heated")` mg/L of dissolved oxygen, against `r est("ysi_do_ambient")` mg/L in ambient tanks. Saturation, the measured concentration as a percentage of what water at equilibrium with air would hold, averaged `r est("ysi_do_pct_heated", 0)`% in heated and `r est("ysi_do_pct_ambient", 0)`% in ambient tanks, and the lowest heated-tank reading was `r sprintf("%.1f", pn("ysi_do_pct_heated")$ci_low)`%. So the spot checks show no low oxygen at the times we sampled, but we did not measure at night, and with four tanks per temperature we cannot test oxygen against coral condition.
- **Does clipping change symbiont loss under heat?** The direction is consistent, but the size isn't settled. Under heat, clipped fragments kept somewhat more symbionts late in the experiment: `r est("zoox_heated_wound_ratio_day10")` times the unclipped mean on Day 10 and `r est("zoox_heated_wound_ratio_day15")` times on Day 15, and more on both days in `r cnt("zoox_heated_tanks_wounded_higher")` of 4 heated tanks. But the model test (`r fF("zoox_temp_x_wound_x_day")`) shifts with which tank we leave out. Each tank holds only one clipped fragment per source patch and day, so tests of clipping × heat are weak. An experiment with more tanks per temperature would settle it.

## Methods details still to add

We need these before the methods are complete. Items marked (Molly) are questions for the field team.

- pH scale of the YSI meter, NBS or total (Molly; asked).
- Whether the daily regeneration scores came from looking at live fragments or from the color-card photos, which exist for only 7 of the 16 days (Molly; asked).
- The observation behind fragment 121's Day 15 radial corallites (Molly).
- Confirmation that we weighed fragments after clipping on Day 0, and what handling the unclipped fragments received on Day 0 (Molly).
- Where on clipped fragments we cut the symbiont biopsy. Molly's draft puts the 1 cm disk between the "tip" and "middle" disks, but clipped fragments have no tip disk (Molly).
- Dark-adaptation time before Fv/Fm readings, and the order of measurements on days with several (Molly).
- Tank volume and feeding (Molly). Light (~200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, 12:12), flow (0.4 L/min) and the collection site (Hauru public beach) are in Molly's draft.
- Whether the daily regeneration scorer knew each fragment's temperature (Molly).
- How the Apex temperature probes were checked, and the time of day of the YSI readings (Molly).
- Whether we planned the source-patch test before seeing the data (for us to write).
- Why we ran the microscope experiment as a separate set of fragments (Molly).
- Why we chose 31 °C and a 15-day run (for us to write).
